title: The Antikythera Mechanism — Ancient Computer, or Just a Toy?
parts: Is the world's most famous ancient computer... actually a broken toy?
In 1901, divers found it inside a 2,000-year-old shipwreck.
For decades, experts called it the first computer ever built.
Now, a new study says that might be wrong.
This is the story of a machine built with more ambition than its own technology could handle.
1900, the island of Simi, Greece.
Sponge divers led by Captain Dimitrios Kontos found a sunken Roman cargo ship.
It had gone down near the island of Antikythera, about 45 meters underwater.
In 1901, they pulled up a corroded lump of bronze and rock.
A year later, researcher Spyridon Stais noticed something odd inside it: a gear.
That single gear was the first clue to what we now call the Antikythera mechanism.
Decades of study followed — X-rays in the 1970s, CT scans in 2005.
What they found: a hand-cranked device packed with bronze gears.
It tracked the Sun and the Moon, and predicted eclipses.
It even followed the calendar of the ancient Greek games, including the Olympics.
Scans suggest it once held around 35 gears. About 30 survive today.
It was built somewhere between 205 and 87 BC — the ship itself sank decades later, around 70 to 60 BC.
Where exactly it was built is still argued over: Corinth, Pergamon, Rhodes. Nobody agrees.
For over a century, the big question was simple: how did ancient Greeks build something this precise?
In 2025, a different question took over.
Did it actually work?
Engineers Esteban Szigety and Gustavo Arenas built a digital simulation of the mechanism.
In their model, the gears kept jamming and slipping out of alignment.
According to their simulation, the device could only run reliably for a few months before breaking down.
Their conclusion: maybe this wasn't a serious scientific instrument at all.
Maybe it was closer to a sophisticated toy — possibly even built for a child.
That's a striking claim. And it hasn't been peer-reviewed yet.
The study's own authors admit only about a third of the original mechanism survives.
Even they say: interpret the results with caution.
Researchers who've studied this machine for years are pushing back.
They argue its sheer complexity makes "just a toy" hard to believe.
One possible explanation: over 2,000 years of corrosion may have distorted the gear measurements the new study relied on.
Here's the thing — the idea that it "didn't work great" isn't actually new.
Researcher Tony Freeth had already concluded, years earlier, that the design outpaced the precision of its own construction.
In his own words, the mechanism "didn't work very well."
So the 2025 debate isn't really "did it work perfectly." Everyone already agreed it didn't.
It's "was this a flawed but serious instrument — or a novelty that was never meant to be taken seriously?"
Nobody has the final answer.
Specialists still argue over exactly how it modeled the planets — no planetary gears survived intact, so every version is a different guess.
Even whether the front dial tracked a 365-day solar year, or a 354-day lunar one, is still argued.
Even which city built it, in the first place.
What we know for certain: over 2,000 years ago, someone tried to build a machine more precise than bronze and hand tools could manage.
Some of history's best-studied objects still change their story every few years.
So next time someone calls this "the first computer," remember — the people who've spent decades studying it still can't agree if it was built to be taken seriously, or to be played with.
What other "ancient breakthrough" might actually be something much simpler than we think?
